What this method does—and what it deliberately does not do

Every visible source pixel is converted from sRGB to linear light and then OKLab. A balanced k-d tree finds the mathematically nearest palette entry in that perceptual space. The output is written as an RGBA PNG, so palettes larger than the 256-entry indexed-PNG limit remain intact.

Floyd–Steinberg mode snakes across alternating rows and diffuses RGB error in linear light. This is more physically sensible than diffusing gamma-encoded sRGB values, although any error diffusion trades local accuracy for a better area-average impression.

OKLab is a strong practical metric, not a perfect visual observer. It does not model viewing conditions, spatial adaptation, or individual color-vision differences. The report above measures direct OKLab error against the original pixels; a dithered image may look smoother even when that number rises.
